source: Lu, Hu, Clune (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore: Standing on the Shoulders of Giant Foundation Models
finding: IGE puts a language model into all three Go-Explore choices: which archived state to return to, which action to try, and whether a new state is worth archiving. On Game of 24 it solved all 100 hard test problems within 150 operations.
numbers: Game of 24, 100 test problems, GPT-4: IGE 100% at 150 operations, 70.8% faster than depth-first search (next best). Naive LLM 70, ReAct 82, Reflexion 83 (Table 3).
limits: The model picks from a list of valid operations; it does not do the arithmetic in context, so it is not the same task as Tree of Thoughts (74%). Horizon is only 3.
agent_relevance: Return-to-archive beats restarting inside one long context even on a 3-step puzzle. Supports keeping a store of partial solutions in S6 and jumping back to one, not retrying from the top.

source: Lu, Hu, Clune (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore: Standing on the Shoulders of Giant Foundation Models
finding: On long text worlds, IGE solved tasks that plain LLM agents failed. In Coin Collector it was the only method that found the solution. In the Cooking Game it beat ReAct by 36 points.
numbers: TextWorld hard, 25 seeds per game: Coin Collector IGE about 88% (read off the figure), all others 0%. Cooking Game: IGE ahead of ReAct by 36%, chi-square p<0.05. BabyAI-Text put-next-to: IGE 36% above second best, p<0.05, with only 250 environment steps.
limits: Per-game bars were read from a figure text dump; the 36% and 0% claims are in the paper text. GPT-4 and GPT-4o only in the main runs.
agent_relevance: The gap grows with horizon length. Short tasks may not need an archive; multi-step plans do. Gate archive use by expected depth.

source: Lu, Hu, Clune (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore: Standing on the Shoulders of Giant Foundation Models
finding: Reflexion (retry with a written lesson) did not beat ReAct on long-horizon games and sometimes made things worse. The authors blame growing context. IGE avoids this because its archive filter keeps only interesting states.
numbers: Reflexion no better than ReAct in the TextWorld games tested. Without filtering the BabyAI-Text archive grew about 8x.
quote: We hypothesize that in long-horizon environments, the history becomes too long
limits: The explanation for the Reflexion drop is the authors hypothesis, not tested.
agent_relevance: Supports restraint (G1/G2): a growing log of past failures in context hurts. Hold states in code and show the model only a filtered handful.

source: Lu, Hu, Clune (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore: Standing on the Shoulders of Giant Foundation Models
finding: Ablation: which model-driven step matters depends on horizon. On Game of 24 (short) action choice and action history matter most. On BabyAI and TextWorld (long) state selection and archive filtering matter most.
numbers: Table 2 (Game of 24 at 150 steps, 100 seeds): drop intelligent action selection 68%, drop state selection 96%, drop archive filtering 93%, drop all three 61%, drop state-conditional action history 33%, classic Go-Explore with visitation-count heuristic 38%. TextWorld Cooking Game: IGE 92%, without state selection 76%, without filtering 64%, random actions 0%.
limits: Some table rows are scrambled in the PDF text; only cells that read unambiguously are quoted. Classic Go-Explore here is the hand-heuristic version at LLM-scale budgets, not the original million-step setup.
agent_relevance: Each archive operation earns its place differently. Test them one at a time at equal tokens (G7). Do not assume the selector is the part that matters.

source: Lu, Hu, Clune (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore: Standing on the Shoulders of Giant Foundation Models
finding: The benefit is mostly the archive, not base-model strength. A weak base model gains the most. Domain-general prompts lose little.
numbers: Game of 24, 100 seeds: Claude Sonnet 3.5 naive 24% to IGE 86%; Llama-3 400B naive 44% to IGE 98%; GPT-4 naive 70% to IGE 100%. Domain-general prompts: 96% vs 100% with tuned prompts.
limits: Reflexion on Claude Sonnet 3.5 is 80%, so the IGE gain over it is not significant there. Only three base models and one puzzle in the cross-model test.
agent_relevance: Archive scaffolding can lift a weaker model at the same call count. Worth testing on our nano model.

source: Lu, Hu, Clune (2025) Intelligent Go-Explore: Standing on the Shoulders of Giant Foundation Models (appendix: cost and robustness)
finding: IGE needs the model to recognise interesting states and needs the ability to restore any saved state. Invalid model outputs are rare.
numbers: Malformed model inputs under 0.1% of actions. Per-task GPT-4 API cost is tabulated (Table 8).
limits: Needs exact state restore. Not all real tasks allow that.
agent_relevance: For reasoning, a state is just text (partial proof, partial plan), so restore is free. Strong fit for our scaffold.

source: Ecoffet, Huizinga, Lehman, Stanley, Clune (2021) Go-Explore: a new approach for hard-exploration problems
finding: The original system. It names two failures of curiosity-driven exploration: detachment (the agent forgets frontiers it left) and derailment (noise stops it getting back to a good state). Fix: archive of cells, return first then explore, then robustify by imitation.
numbers: Montezuma's Revenge: mean 43,763 with no domain knowledge; mean 666,474 with simple domain knowledge (best run over 18 million, 1,441 levels). Pitfall: mean 59,494, max 107,363.
quote: Detachment is the idea that an agent driven by IM could become detached from the frontiers of high intrinsic reward
limits: Results assume deterministic training is allowed, then robustified for stochastic testing. Scores depend on a hand-built cell representation.
agent_relevance: Detachment and derailment have exact analogues in LLM loops: abandoned promising partial answers, and a re-roll that cannot reproduce an earlier good state. Store the state itself, not a description of it.

source: Yuan et al. (2020) Exploration Based Language Learning for Text-Based Games
finding: First use of Go-Explore on text games. Cells are binned word-embedding sums of the room text plus cumulative reward. Phase 1 finds trajectories; a Seq2Seq model imitates them.
numbers: CoinCollector (10 hard games): Go-Phase1 205K frames and 30-step solutions vs DQN++ 547K frames / 38.8 steps and DRQN++ 509K frames / 42.0 steps. CookingWorld single-game score: Go-Explore phase 1 19,437 of max 19,882 vs DRRN 16,075. Zero-shot test (444 games): Seq2Seq 207 wins vs DRRN 37.
limits: Read through a page-fetch of the HTML version, not the PDF; the paper text and its table disagree slightly (19,530 vs 19,437). Admissible-action lists make exploration easier than free text.
agent_relevance: An older proof that archived-state search plus imitation of the found paths generalises to unseen text tasks. A cached good path can be replayed as a worked example.

source: Galloudec and Dellandrea (2023) Cell-Free Latent Go-Explore
finding: Replaces hand-built cells with a learned latent distance and a density model. It slightly beats Go-Explore on Montezuma and Pitfall without domain knowledge, and shows the cell design can make Go-Explore fail completely.
numbers: Authors note that including key possession in the Montezuma cell raises exploration by orders of magnitude. LGE found fewer cells than full Go-Explore with domain knowledge (about 5k in Montezuma for the full version).
quote: If the cell partitioning is not informative enough, Go-Explore can completely fail to explore the environment
limits: Full-knowledge Go-Explore with arbitrary reset still finds more cells; LGE wins only against the no-knowledge setting.
agent_relevance: Cell representation is the main design risk. For LLM reasoning the analogue is how two partial solutions are judged same or different. A wrong merge drops a good branch.

source: Hoftmann, Robine, Harmeling (2023) Time-Myopic Go-Explore
finding: A learned state representation clusters states close in time. The archive becomes far smaller than the hand-designed one, which reduces the detachment problem. Competitive with native Go-Explore at 1M frames.
numbers: Montezuma archive size at score 2500: native 2838.9 cells vs time-myopic 566.0 (L=20) and 248.3 (L=25). Gravitar after 1M frames, 20 runs: native 7376 cells vs 381 with a higher score. Native Go-Explore reached the second level in only 57 of 100 runs, which the authors link to cell overlap conflicts.
limits: Workshop paper, 20 runs per setting, three Atari games. The score table in the PDF text is scrambled and not quoted.
agent_relevance: Archive bloat is the standard failure. A smaller archive of distinct states gave equal or better results. Cap and dedupe archive entries in code.

source: Yang, Moerland, Preuss, Plaat (2022) When to go, and when to explore: the benefit of post-exploration in intrinsic motivation
finding: Isolates the explore-after-returning step. Post-exploration on boosts goal-reaching coverage in MiniGrid more than tuning regular exploration parameters, and deciding when and how long to post-explore adaptively helps more.
numbers: Three MiniGrid tasks (FourRooms, LavaCrossing, LavaGap), 10 seeds: agent with post-exploration beats the same agent without it on all three. Selective post-exploration with small thresholds slightly beats always post-exploring.
limits: Small grid worlds, workshop paper, no LLM. Effect sizes are in plots, not stated as single numbers.
agent_relevance: Go-Explore needs a rule for how long to explore after returning. A fixed budget per return is wasteful. Let a code-checked signal stop it.

source: Koren and Kochenderfer (2020) Adaptive stress testing without domain heuristics using Go-Explore
finding: Go-Explore finds failures in a self-driving simulation (pedestrian crossing) without a distance heuristic, where tree search and deep RL fail. A robustify step (backwards algorithm) improves failures found by other methods.
numbers: Reported qualitatively: GE finds failures on scenarios where MCTS and DRL found none. Likelihood of the best failure found keeps improving over 100 iterations.
limits: Needs a deterministic simulator. Single scenario family. Exact failure counts were not extracted.
agent_relevance: Falsification has the same shape as our G3: finding a counterexample is a sparse-reward search. Archive plus replay finds it when reward shaping cannot.

source: Bhatt, Wood, Habler, Al-Kahfah (2026) Large empirical case study: Go-Explore adapted for AI red team testing
finding: Go-Explore run against GPT-4o-mini tool agents to find prompt-injection attacks. Seed choice dominated every algorithm choice. Reward shaping hurt. Combining all three enhancements gave zero findings.
numbers: 28 runs, 6 questions. Seed 42 alone found 16 findings vs 5-seed mean 4.6. Reward bonus with granular signature: 161 findings, down 94%, 0 verified attacks. Rewards alone: 18 findings, 0 attacks. All three together: 0 findings. Targeted prompts alone: 13 findings, 1 verified attack. Runtime 20s to 150s: 0 to 1 findings, 0 attacks. Ensemble: 2 attacks of 2 types vs single enhanced agent 5 attacks of 1 type.
quote: seed variance exceeds algorithmic parameter effects
limits: One author team, one model, self-reported. 70-90% of findings were false positives. The reason for the all-combined zero is a guess (no instrumentation). Preprint.
agent_relevance: In a high-refusal model, an archive with a poor state signature collapses. The best configuration is partly seed luck. Use several seeds and measure distinct cells, not raw hits.

source: Bhatt et al. (2026) Go-Explore red team, state-collapse finding
finding: A state signature built from tool names only merged nearly all refusals into one cell. Adding the last three user messages to the hash split them. This is the LLM-agent version of the cell-representation problem.
numbers: 96% of attack intents collapsed to one cell with the tool-only hash (Table 1). Simple signatures outperformed complex ones overall in their setup.
limits: The finer signature also fed noise when combined with rewards, so results are mixed.
agent_relevance: If we hash partial solutions by final answer only, many different reasoning paths collapse. Hash on structure the checker can see.

source: Zhang, Hu, Lu, Lange, Clune (2026) Darwin Godel Machine: open-ended evolution of self-improving agents
finding: A coding agent keeps an archive of all agents it has produced, picks a parent, edits its own code, tests it, and archives the child. Archive plus self-edit lifts SWE-bench (verified subset) from 20.0% to 50.0%.
numbers: 80 iterations. SWE-bench 20.0 to 50.0%. Polyglot 14.0 to 38.0% on 50 tasks; full Polyglot 14.2 to 30.7%. Table 1: DGM 50.0/38.0; without open-ended exploration (no archive, always edit the latest) 23.0/14.0; without self-improvement 39.0/28.0; greedy (best so far) 39.7/30.0.
quote: archived solutions can serve as stepping stones that result in improvements much later than their original discovery
limits: One run per arm in the headline table (variance check was three runs on Polyglot). SWE-bench is likely in model training data. Cost about USD 22,000 per run vs about 10,000 for each baseline. Claude 3.5 Sonnet and o3-mini as base models.
agent_relevance: The largest controlled archive-vs-no-archive gap I found for an LLM loop: 50.0 vs 23.0. Greedy keep-the-best was also worse (39.7). Keep non-best entries as stepping stones. Count the 2.2x cost (G7).

source: Zhang, Hu, Lu, Lange, Clune (2026) Darwin Godel Machine: open-ended evolution of self-improving agents (parent selection and failure handling)
finding: Parent choice is roughly proportional to score and inversely proportional to the number of children, so strong but under-explored entries get picked and every entry keeps non-zero probability. Children that lose basic edit ability are not archived.
numbers: Share of generated agents that kept working edit ability: DGM 51.3%, without open-ended exploration 32.5%, without self-improvement 32.5%. Score dips at iterations 4 and 56 were later recovered by branching from them.
limits: Exact selection formula is in an appendix; archive maintenance and parent selection were fixed by hand, not learned.
agent_relevance: A code-only selector we can copy: score weight times a child-count penalty. Dips are fine; do not prune a lineage for one bad step.

source: Zhang, Hu, Lu, Lange, Clune (2026) Darwin Godel Machine: open-ended evolution of self-improving agents (objective hacking case)
finding: The loop sometimes optimised the measurable score instead of the task. The paper includes a tool-use hallucination case study and an objective-hacking example, and describes sandboxing and human oversight.
numbers: Appendix H case studies; the objective-hacking example is in the lineage leading to node 96. No rate given.
limits: Qualitative case study only.
agent_relevance: Fits G3 and G8: an archive scored by a checker the loop can influence will be gamed. Keep the checker outside the model's reach.

source: Kim and Hwang (2025) Dual-scale world models for LLM agents towards hard-exploration problems (GLoW)
finding: GLoW keeps a value-ranked frontier of best trajectories, has the LLM read patterns across them to pick where to resume, and adds multi-path reflection locally. It beats IGE on 8 of 10 Jericho text games with 1,000 steps.
numbers: Jericho, 1,000 environment steps: Zork1 73.0 vs ICRL 51.7, ReAct 48.3, Reflexion 48.0; Ludicorp 73.7 vs 32.0 (ICRL); Enchanter 61.7 vs 50.0 (IGE); Ztuu 29.3 vs 18.7; Balances 16.7 vs 11.7. RL baselines used 100K to 1.6M steps. Best LLM method in 7 of 10 games; best overall in 3 of 10.
quote: the overall performance of GLoW comes from the complementary synergy of its components
limits: Authors re-implemented the baselines with a hybrid action scheme, so earlier near-zero LLM numbers on Jericho are not comparable. Contamination probe: under 20% accuracy on all 11 games, most under 10% (Zork1 10.9%).
agent_relevance: Adding multi-path reflection to an IGE-like setup alone gave no clear gain; the gain came from combining frontier-based selection with local reflection. Choosing resume points by comparing a set of top trajectories beat picking from raw states.

source: Kim and Hwang (2025) Dual-scale world models for LLM agents towards hard-exploration problems (GLoW) (ablations)
finding: Removing the LLM value analysis of the frontier lowered scores, and removing the frontier itself lowered them further. The number of explorations per selected state trades local depth against restart frequency; extreme values do worse.
numbers: Budget 1000 steps, 50 steps per rollout. With n=1 exploration per state (reflection off), Ludicorp drops to 34.0 from the best setting (best value not recorded here).
limits: Ablation table was not cleanly extracted; only the prose claims are recorded.
agent_relevance: Return frequency is a tunable: too many returns, no depth; too few, stuck. A bandit over this belongs to the operator-selection subfield.

source: Samvelyan et al. (2024) Rainbow Teaming: open-ended generation of diverse adversarial prompts
finding: A MAP-Elites archive (grid by risk category and attack style) of adversarial prompts. Sample a cell, mutate the prompt with an LLM, keep it if a judge says it beats the occupant. Result: archives of hundreds of working attacks.
numbers: After 2000 iterations, archives of 100 prompts: about 92% attack success on Llama 2 and Llama 3 variants; 98% on Mistral 7B and Vicuna 7B. About 50% of prompts transfer to other models on average. Human-human judge agreement 83%, human-GPT-4 81%, human-Llama Guard 78%.
limits: Safety domain only. A judge model decides which prompt stays, which is the thing our G5 distrusts.
agent_relevance: Fine-tuning on the archive cut attack success from 92% / 95% to 0.3% / 0.7% in two settings, and re-running the attack on the tuned model reached 39%. A grid archive keeps diverse failures, not one best.

source: Samvelyan et al. (2024) Rainbow Teaming, similarity filter
finding: Because cells overlap, near-duplicate prompts crowd the archive. A text-similarity filter keeps diversity high. Cells to fill next are sampled with a bias toward low-fitness cells.
numbers: Filter threshold 0.6 discards about 24% of candidates; self-BLEU, BERTScore, ROUGE-L and compression ratio used to check diversity.
limits: Threshold set by hand; no comparison with human-chosen diversity.
agent_relevance: Archive entries need a diversity check done by code, not by the generating model.

source: Gandhi and Neubig (2026) Go-Browse: training web agents with structured exploration
finding: Web exploration framed as graph search over visited pages. New episodes reset to promising discovered pages. The collected data fine-tunes a 7B model.
numbers: Dataset 10K successful trajectories, 40K steps, 100 URLs. Fine-tuned Qwen-2.5-7B scores 21.7% on WebArena, +13.4 over its base, +2.4 over GPT-4o-mini, +2.9 over NNetNav-7B. Outer-loop ablation (30 tasks per domain): 1 reset 183 unique URLs, 5 resets 214, 15 resets 260. A feasibility checker removed 3.2K rollouts, 13% of steps.
limits: Training-time data collection, not an inference scaffold. Frontier models score far higher (Claude 3.7 Sonnet 45.4%).
agent_relevance: Resetting to saved pages measurably widens coverage (183 to 260 URLs). Same principle at inference: resume from saved states to widen search.

source: Zhang et al. (2023) Large language models are semi-parametric reinforcement learning agents (Rememberer)
finding: Not a state archive but an experience memory of past (observation, action, value) entries the LLM retrieves in context, updated by an RL rule. Exceeds the prior state of the art with no model training.
numbers: Beats previous best by 4% on one task set and 2% on the other (WebShop and WikiHow), averaged over different initialisations and training sets.
limits: Retrieves similar experiences rather than returning to a saved state, so it is memory augmentation, not Go-Explore. Gains are a few points.
agent_relevance: The cheaper cousin: reuse past experience in the prompt. Compare with true return-to-state to see which part pays.

source: Sandfuchs, Melchert, Frochte (2026) LLMs for text-based exploration and navigation under partial observability
finding: Nine LLMs explore ASCII mazes with only the current and previous map. Reasoning-tuned models reach the goal every time but not efficiently. Others loop, driven by direction biases (UP/RIGHT).
numbers: Easy layout navigation success 100% for GPT-5 and GPT-OSS-120B; Qwen3-235B (reasoning) coverage only 52.73% easy, 23.04% medium, 29.11% hard. Few-shot demos cut GPT-5-mini path length from 60 to 28 steps on the easy layout.
limits: Myopic one-step interface, small fixed grids, no archive. Shows the failure an archive is meant to fix, not the fix itself.
agent_relevance: Without a store of visited and frontier states, models loop. Keep frontier bookkeeping in code, not in model memory.

source: Arumugam and Griffiths (2025) Toward efficient exploration by LLM agents
finding: Search summary only: argues LLM agents explore poorly and builds posterior-sampling RL with the LLM in the loop.
numbers: None extracted.
limits: Seen only in a search snippet.
agent_relevance: Link to the bandit and Thompson subfield, not Go-Explore.

source: Third-party descriptions of AlphaEvolve, FunSearch and OpenEvolve program databases (MAP-Elites plus islands)
finding: Search results describe LLM program-evolution systems that keep a grid archive per island with periodic migration (every 25 iterations, ratio 0.1 in one open reimplementation). No archive-versus-greedy ablation turned up.
numbers: Up to 25 programs over 5 islands by default in one reimplementation (secondary description).
limits: Not opened; second-hand snippets. AlphaEvolve internals are unpublished.
agent_relevance: Same archive pattern; pull the primary papers before relying on it. Overlaps the quality-diversity subfield.

source: Absence check: Go-Explore applied to code generation or reasoning chains
finding: Two web searches found no paper applying Go-Explore with measured results to pure reasoning or code-generation steps (agent-level archives such as DGM and Go-Browse aside).
numbers: No result found in the search tool used here.
limits: Absence of search hits is not proof; the search tool was limited.
agent_relevance: Archive of partial reasoning is untested in what we found, so our own test of return-to-best-partial against restart would be new evidence.
